facts.statement: Thomas Hawkins acquired the remains of Eurycleidus in the early 1830s from a quarry in Street, Somerset, and described them in 1834.
facts.quote: They were acquired by Thomas Hawkins during the early 1830s from a quarry in Street, Somerset and he described them in 1834.

facts.statement: Charles William Andrews named the genus Eurycleidus in 1922 after re-preparing and exposing the pectoral girdle of the specimen originally known as Plesiosaurus arcuatus.
facts.quote: In 1922, after the pectoral girdle had been re-prepared and exposed, Charles William Andrews named the genus Eurycleidus for Plesiosaurus arcuatus.

facts.statement: The genus Eurycleidus contains only one currently accepted species, E. arcuatus.
facts.quote: It contains a single species, E. arcuatus.

facts.statement: Most phylogenetic analyses classify Eurycleidus arcuatus as a relatively basal member of the family Rhomaleosauridae.
facts.quote: Most phylogenetic analyses find the type species of the genus, Plesiosaurus arcuatus Owen 1840, with as combinatio nova Eurycleidus arcuatus Andrews 1922, to be a relatively basal rhomaleosaurid.

facts.statement: Eurycleidus lived during the Hettangian to Pliensbachian stages of the Early Jurassic, approximately 201.4 to 184.2 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Hettangian to Pliensbachian (201.4 to 184.2 million years ago)

facts.statement: Eurycleidus likely fed on fish, catching them with its sharp, needle-like teeth.
facts.quote: Like other plesiosaurs, Eurycleidus probably lived on a diet of fish, using its sharp needle-like teeth to catch prey.

facts.statement: Eurycleidus possessed large shoulder bones that indicate it was capable of powerful forward strokes for fast swimming.
facts.quote: Its shoulder bones were fairly large, indicating a powerful forward stroke for fast swimming.

facts.statement: It is debated whether E. megacephalus belongs to Eurycleidus; while Smith (2007) reassigned it to the genus, most analyses suggest it represents a distinct, unnamed genus separate from Eurycleidus and Rhomaleosaurus.
facts.quote: A second species, E. megacephalus (Stutchbury, 1846 [originally Rhomaleosaurus megacephalus]), was reassigned to this genus by Smith (2007). However, most analyses find E. megacephalus to represent an unnamed genus, which is distinct from both Eurycleidus and Rhomaleosaurus.

facts.statement: A specimen from Halberstadt, Germany, originally assigned to Eurycleidus arcuatus, was moved to the distinct genus Lindwurmia in 2019.
facts.quote: A specimen discovered in 1899 in Halberstadt, Germany that was assigned to Eurycleidus arcuatus was moved to its own genus Lindwurmia in 2019.
